subject: Biotechnology
title: Human Cloning Ethics
description: Learn Human Cloning Ethics in one minute.

hook.text: Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996 — the question immediately arose: could humans be next? Should they?

buildup.text: Reproductive cloning creates a genetic copy — therapeutic cloning creates embryonic stem cells for medicine, not a person.

discovery.text: Over 70 countries ban reproductive human cloning — but therapeutic cloning regulations vary widely across the globe.

twist.text: Induced pluripotent stem cells bypass the cloning debate — adult cells reprogrammed to stem cells need no embryos at all.

climax.text: The UN failed to pass a binding treaty on human cloning — a non-binding declaration was adopted instead in 2005.

punchline.text: Clone a sheep, debate a century — human cloning remains biotech's ultimate taboo.

quiz.question: How did induced pluripotent stem cells change the cloning ethics debate?
options: They made human reproductive cloning safe and ethical
They provided an alternative to therapeutic cloning that creates stem cells from adult cells without embryos
They proved that human cloning is technically impossible

details.summary: Human reproductive cloning, creating a genetic copy of an existing person, is banned virtually worldwide due to extreme safety risks and profound ethical objections. Therapeutic cloning to produce stem cells raises separate but related ethical debates about embryo status.
details.whyItMatters: Cloning technology exists in animals but remains too dangerous and ethically fraught for human application. The debate established important precedents for how society governs powerful biotechnologies before they become practical.
takeaways: Reproductive human cloning is banned in virtually every country
Animal cloning success rates remain low with high rates of abnormalities
Therapeutic cloning for stem cells is permitted in some countries

faq.question: Why is human reproductive cloning considered unethical?
faq.answer: Animal cloning produces high rates of developmental abnormalities, stillbirth, and early death. Applying this to humans would be reckless. Beyond safety, cloning raises concerns about identity, treating children as products, and undermining human individuality and dignity.

faq.question: What is the difference between reproductive and therapeutic cloning?
faq.answer: Reproductive cloning aims to create a new person genetically identical to the donor. Therapeutic cloning creates cloned embryos only to harvest stem cells for medical treatment, with no intent to implant them. The embryo is destroyed in the process, which raises separate ethical concerns.
